page1.title: Where do the patterns come from?
page1.subtitle: After predicting the next token, you might wonder: How did the model learn that some continuations are more likely than others?
page1.lesson4: The model is exposed to many different pieces of text.
page1.lesson5: Across these examples, it learns patterns in which tokens tend to appear in similar situations.
page1.intro: Before you start chatting with a model, it has already learned patterns from a very large number of training examples.
page1.targetCovered: Later, those learned patterns help with next-token prediction.
page1.technical: The process in which a model learns patterns from many examples before it is used for prediction.
page1.takeaway: From many examples like these, the model can learn that some tokens are more likely to follow certain patterns than others.

page2.title: How does the model improve a prediction?
page2.subtitle: A correction signal nudges many adjustable numbers by tiny amounts.
page2.manyNumbers: These controls stand for many adjustable numbers working together—not one slot for each word.
page2.oneExample: The target Token becomes more likely for this example, one small step at a time.
page2.technical: A parameter is one of the many adjustable numbers inside a model. During training, many parameters are changed by tiny amounts.
page2.weight: Loss measures the prediction gap. A gradient tells the optimiser which small parameter changes would reduce it.
page2.takeaway: Compare with the real target, measure the gap, adjust many parameters a little, then repeat across many examples.
page2.definition: A regular way that words or Tokens tend to appear together in many examples.
page2.introBody: These sentences all have similar situations.
page2.patternCopy: Across many examples, the model learns that some Tokens tend to appear together more often than others.
page2.chartTitle: Example: The next word after “opened the book”
page2.takeawayTitle: The model is learning statistical patterns from many examples.
page2.takeawayBody: It is not just storing one sentence to look up later.

page3.title: Why does training use so many examples?
page3.subtitle: Watch the predict, reveal, compare and adjust loop repeat across existing text.
page3.allProcessed: All four examples passed through the loop.
page3.technical: Generalisation means learned numerical patterns can help with new combinations of text. Training is not simply a database of complete sentences.
page3.takeaway: One example changes the model only a little. Repeating the loop across huge amounts of text gradually shapes useful prediction patterns.
page3.definition: A regular way that Tokens tend to appear in similar situations, learned from many training examples.
page3.introLine1: During training, the model has seen many examples.
page3.introLine2: From these, it learns patterns about which Tokens often appear in similar situations.
page3.flowAria: Many examples lead to learned patterns that shape a later prediction
page3.patternAria: Abstract learned pattern centred on read
page3.stage3Line1: Later, when it sees a similar context,
page3.stage3Line2: it uses the patterns it has learned.
page3.takeawayTitle: These probabilities did not appear from nowhere.
page3.takeawayBody: They are shaped by patterns the model learned across many training examples.

page6.q1Prompt: Where do the patterns used in an LLM’s later predictions mainly come from?
page6.q1A: From many examples used during training.
page6.q1B: From the last sentence the user typed.
page6.q1C: From a list of fixed answers stored for every question.
page6.q1D: From randomly choosing words each time.
page6.q1Correct: During training, the model learns statistical patterns across many examples. Those learned patterns can later influence its predictions.
page6.q1Incorrect: Think back to the start of Lesson 5: the model learned patterns before normal use by training on many examples.
page6.q2Prompt: What does it mean when we say the model learns a “pattern”?
page6.q2A: It stores every training sentence as one complete answer.
page6.q2B: It learns recurring statistical relationships across many examples.
page6.q2C: It learns one grammar rule for every sentence.
page6.q2D: It remembers only the most recent training example.
page6.q2Correct: Exactly. A pattern is a recurring relationship learned across many examples, not simply one sentence saved for later lookup.
page6.q2Incorrect: Remember Page 2: training is not just storing one whole example. The model learns recurring statistical relationships across many examples.
page6.q3Prompt: During training, what can happen after the model compares its prediction with what appeared in the training example?
page6.q3A: The whole model is completely retrained from scratch.
page6.q3B: Some internal parameters can be adjusted a little.
page6.q3C: The model immediately becomes perfect after one example.
page6.q3D: The example is copied directly into every future answer.
page6.q3Correct: One training step can make a small adjustment to internal parameters. Training repeats this across many examples.
page6.q3Incorrect: One example does not teach the whole model. The important idea is: small adjustments repeated many times.
page6.q4Prompt: Why might a next-token probability change after a model has learned from many training examples?
page6.q4A: Learned patterns can shape which next tokens become more likely later.
page6.q4B: The model always chooses the token that appeared most recently.
page6.q4C: Training makes every possible token equally likely.
page6.q4D: The model searches its training data for the exact same sentence before every prediction.
page6.q4Correct: Yes! This is the key connection: training examples → learned patterns → later predictions.
page6.q4Incorrect: Think about the tiny toy model: changing the training examples changed the learned pattern, which changed the later prediction.
